gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, when a named reviewer measured the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2, it gave 231 Wh from AC (80% of its 288 Wh) and its inverter used about 19 W with nothing plugged in (The Technology Man, UK unit), while Techtest measured 273 Wh (95%) from the DC-only Anker SOLIX C300X DC.
standout_why: I opened all five rival pages that ChatGPT cited: solar-home.space, campequipmentplus.com, solutionenergy.com, energysage.com and popsci.com. None of them reports a measured figure. Every number on them is a maker spec, a retailer listing or the site's own arithmetic. SolutionEnergy and EnergySage assume a generic 85% usable capacity. EnergySage says it 'did not test these models'. PopSci says it hasn't tested the v2 Jackery units. None of them gives a measured usable capacity, idle draw or real panel wattage for any candidate.
decides: These figures support the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 + 100 W kit for phones, lights, a fan and a laptop. They also show that our 'CPAP one night' cell is too optimistic for the AC outlet. The Technology Man measured 231 Wh from AC and about 19 W of inverter idle draw. Over an 8-hour night that idle draw alone is about 150 Wh. A 30 W CPAP running 8 hours needs 240 Wh, which is more than the 231 Wh measured from AC. A CPAP should run from the DC output, where the same reviewer measured 244 Wh. For shoppers who only run USB and 12 V gear, the C300X DC gave about 42 Wh more usable energy than the Elite 30 V2 did on AC (273 vs 231 Wh). On real panel output: Macworld got about 30 W from Jackery's 40 W panel on the Explorer 300 Plus. That supports the line on our page that the 40 W panel adds little.
candidates: Jackery Solar Generator 1000 v2 (Explorer 1000 v2 + 200 W)
